title: Taking Managed Instances through design, security and rollout
question: Tell me about a time you drove a technical initiative

situation: AWS introduced Managed Instances for Lambda, allowing customers to run functions on EC2 infrastructure while retaining Lambda's managed scaling and execution model. Our Code Management & Optimization team needed to extend its packaging and artifact-management services to support this new execution tier.
The initiative crossed several control-plane and data-plane services, with security and operational-readiness requirements that were not simply a variation of the existing Lambda On-Demand path.
task: I took ownership of my team's part of the initiative: defining the high-level design, driving the implementation and operational-readiness review, coordinating the integration with partner services, and acting as the technical point of contact of my team for the control and data planes.
action: I worked with limited input from the global technical lead to establish the initial architecture and break the work down across the different service boundaries and dependencies.

My initial design deliberately stayed close to Lambda On-Demand, with the goal of making the two execution models as interchangeable as possible. This gave us a familiar architecture and reduced the amount of new behaviour we had to introduce.

About two months into the project, with roughly 75% of the implementation complete, I became concerned that this alignment was forcing us into a weaker artifact-security model. I revisited the security requirements and concluded that dedicated artifact encryption at rest was the stronger long-term design.

Rather than continue with a design I no longer believed in because we had already invested heavily in it, I presented the trade-off, drove the architectural change, and reworked the core components around the new security model while keeping the delivery timeline intact.

I then coordinated the integration with multiple control-plane and data-plane dependencies, drove the operational-readiness work, and established validation pipelines that allowed us to deploy our changes without customer impact.
result: The team's implementation and operational-readiness requirements landed on schedule with zero customer impact, providing support for Managed Instances across our service.

The final design also gave us a stronger security boundary around customer artifacts rather than preserving architectural similarity with On-Demand at the expense of the new execution model's requirements.

challenge: The most challenging part was changing direction after the original architecture was already roughly 75% implemented. The technical challenge was significant, but the harder part was recognising that the existing direction was no longer the right one and taking responsibility for changing it without allowing the project timeline to slip.
hardestBug: The hardest issues were cross-service failures during joint testing. Our service depended on several control-plane and data-plane components, so an end-to-end failure did not immediately identify which service was responsible. I had to isolate individual dependencies, reproduce the failure paths, and use targeted validation to establish where the fault actually originated.
differently: I would bring the security and compliance review into the architecture phase earlier. The original design was strongly influenced by our desire to stay aligned with Lambda On-Demand, and an earlier explicit review of the differences between the two execution models would have surfaced the artifact-encryption requirement before implementation was well underway.
aboutYourself: I learned that I am comfortable challenging my own decisions, even when changing direction has a significant cost. Once I had enough evidence that the original architecture was not the right long-term choice, I was willing to absorb the rework rather than defend a design simply because I had already invested in it.
enjoyed: I enjoyed owning the system design end to end: understanding the different service boundaries, reasoning through the security and data-flow implications, and working with partner teams to turn the architecture into a production-ready system.
